consensus_summary: The consensus identifies the new moon as Israel’s lunar month-opening calendrical and cultic observance, commonly associated with renewal and, in Christian typology, treated as a ceremonial shadow fulfilled in Christ. It generally does not define the exact lunar phase, though ordinary historical views favor conjunction or the first visible crescent.
book_summary: The book likewise identifies the new moon as the lunar phase beginning the month, but specifically reclassifies the full moon—associated with the east gate and appointed times—as that phase, explicitly contrasting it with conjunction or the first visible crescent.
consensus_core_identification: The lunar marker and sacred observance that begins each biblical month.
book_core_identification: The full moon as the lunar marker that begins each biblical month.
boundary_disagreement: The book excludes the dark conjunction and first visible crescent from the month-opening referent and assigns that role to the full moon. Thus it preserves the consensus category of a month-opening lunar marker while materially changing which lunar phase belongs within it.
material_contradiction: The full-moon identification conflicts with the commonly accepted conjunction/crescent identification: these phases cannot all be the unique beginning of the same lunar month in the same calendrical system. This is a boundary-level reclassification rather than replacement of the central lunar-calendar referent.
rationale: Both readings center on a lunar phase marking the start of the month, so the book does not replace the consensus’s basic referent. Its distinctive claim is the precise phase: full moon rather than conjunction or crescent. That materially changes the cases covered and therefore makes the relationship REFINED rather than MATCH. It is not NOVEL because the month-opening lunar-marker category is plainly represented in the consensus, and not DIVERGENT because that central category remains intact.
strongest_objection: The printed passages establish recurring new-moon worship, feasting, monthly timing, and the opening of Ezekiel’s east-facing temple gate, but none unambiguously states that the new moon is the full moon. Psalm 81:3’s KJV phrase “in the time appointed” may be used for that inference, yet the excerpts alone do not demonstrate it, and Ezekiel’s east gate is directly a temple gate rather than an explicit astronomical location of the moon.
